CALIFORNIA INTESTATE SUCCESSION DISTRIBUTION SHARES (PROB. CODE §§ 6400-6402) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Jordan Lee is reviewing this information sheet in connection with the estate of Pat Morgan. This sheet explains, on a general informational basis only, California's default statutory scheme for dividing a decedent's property when all or part of the decedent's estate is not effectively disposed of by a valid will — Probate Code §§ 6400–6402 — including the surviving spouse's or registered domestic partner's statutory share and the order in which other relatives inherit when there is no surviving spouse or registered domestic partner, or for whatever part of the estate does not pass to one. This sheet states general facts about how California's intestate succession statutes are written. It does not determine Pat Morgan's heirs, does not characterize any specific item of Pat Morgan's property as community, quasi-community, or separate property, and does not advise Jordan Lee or anyone else on what to do about any actual estate.

WHEN CALIFORNIA'S INTESTATE SUCCESSION RULES APPLY
California Probate Code § 6400 provides that any part of a decedent's estate not effectively disposed of by a valid will passes to the decedent's heirs as prescribed in Probate Code Division 6, Part 2 (§§ 6400–6455) — the intestate succession statutes. Whether Pat Morgan's estate is governed in whole or in part by these statutes depends on whether Pat Morgan left a valid will and, if so, whether that will disposed of all of Pat Morgan's property; property a will fails to reach — because the will is invalid, silent as to that particular asset, or covers only part of the estate — passes under this same intestate framework even where a will governs the rest of the estate. This information sheet describes the statutory shares set out in Probate Code §§ 6401 and 6402: the surviving spouse's or registered domestic partner's intestate share, and the shares of other relatives when there is no surviving spouse or registered domestic partner, or for whatever portion of separate property does not pass to one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any part of the estate of a decedent not effectively disposed of by will passes to the decedent’s heirs as prescribed in this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6400 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6400 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6400.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, Prob. Code § 6400, used as evidence of the basic trigger for California's intestate succession framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. This is a single statutory section; no other independent source is cited in this clause. Neither § 6400 nor this clause addresses how a court or personal representative determines whether a particular document is a valid will or resolves a dispute over whether a will effectively disposes of specific property — those are separate questions this document does not cover.

THE SURVIVING SPOUSE'S OR DOMESTIC PARTNER'S SHARE OF SEPARATE PROPERTY
Probate Code § 6401(c) sets the surviving spouse's or registered domestic partner's intestate share of a decedent's separate property — property that is neither community nor quasi-community property — on a sliding scale that depends on which other relatives survive the decedent. The surviving spouse or domestic partner takes the entire intestate estate if the decedent leaves no surviving issue (children, grandchildren, and other descendants), parent, sibling, or issue of a deceased sibling. The share drops to one-half of the intestate estate if the decedent leaves only one child, or the issue of one deceased child, or if the decedent leaves no issue but leaves a parent or parents (or their issue). The share drops further, to one-third of the intestate estate, if the decedent leaves more than one child, one child together with the issue of one or more other deceased children, or the issue of two or more deceased children. This separate-property scale is distinct from the surviving spouse's or domestic partner's share of community and quasi-community property, which — as documented elsewhere in this corpus — is simply the one-half of that property that already belonged to the decedent under Probate Code §§ 100 and 101, confirmed as the surviving spouse's or domestic partner's intestate share of that property by § 6401(a)-(b).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(c) As to separate property, the intestate share of the surviving spouse is as follows: (1) The entire intestate estate if the decedent did not leave any surviving issue, parent, brother, sister, or issue of a deceased brother or sister. (2) One-half of the intestate estate in the following cases: (A) Where the decedent leaves only one child or the issue of one deceased child. (B) Where the decedent leaves no issue, but leaves a parent or parents or their issue or the issue of either of them. (3) One-third of the intestate estate in the following cases: (A) Where the decedent leaves more than one child. (B) Where the decedent leaves one child and the issue of one or more deceased children. (C) Where the decedent leaves issue of two or more deceased children."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6401(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6401(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6401.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate or which state's law determines whether specific property is separate property. This clause quotes only subdivision (c) of § 6401; subdivisions (a) and (b), addressing the surviving spouse's or domestic partner's share of community and quasi-community property, are independently quoted and verified elsewhere in this corpus (at the commprop_no_administration_rule clause) and are not re-quoted here so as not to duplicate that existing citation, though this clause's body describes what they provide. Section 6401's own text uses the term "surviving spouse" without separately restating "registered domestic partner" within this particular section; the extension of spousal intestate-succession treatment to a registered domestic partner rests on other Probate Code provisions (including §§ 37, 100, and 101 — the latter two independently verified elsewhere in this corpus) that this clause does not itself re-verify. This clause does not address § 6402.5's special rule for property attributable to a predeceased spouse or domestic partner, which this document does not cover.

DISTRIBUTION TO DESCENDANTS, OR TO PARENTS, WHEN THERE IS NO SURVIVING SPOUSE OR PARTNER
Probate Code § 6402 governs the part of a decedent's intestate estate that does not pass to a surviving spouse or registered domestic partner under § 6401 — and, where there is no surviving spouse or domestic partner at all, the entire intestate estate. Except as provided in a separate statute this document does not cover (§ 6402.5, addressing property attributable to a predeceased spouse or domestic partner), § 6402 first sends that property to the decedent's issue — children, and more remote descendants such as grandchildren — with issue of the same degree of kinship to the decedent taking equal shares, and issue of a more remote degree taking their shares "by representation" under a separate statute, Probate Code § 240, that this document does not independently cover. Only if the decedent leaves no surviving issue does § 6402(b) send that property to the decedent's parent or parents, in equal shares between them if both survive.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as provided in Section 6402.5, the part of the intestate estate not passing to the surviving spouse, under Section 6401, or the entire intestate estate if there is no surviving spouse, passes as follows: (a) To the issue of the decedent, the issue taking equally if they are all of the same degree of kinship to the decedent, but if of unequal degree those of more remote degree take in the manner provided in Section 240. (b) If there is no surviving issue, to the decedent’s parent or parents equally."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6402, introductory clause and subdivisions (a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6402(a)-(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6402.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, Prob. Code § 6402, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. This clause quotes the section's introductory sentence together with subdivisions (a) and (b); subdivisions (c) through (g), addressing more remote relatives, are quoted in the two clauses that follow this one in this document rather than repeated here, so that no subdivision of § 6402 is quoted more than once across this document. Probate Code § 240's "by representation" method of dividing shares among descendants of unequal degree, and § 6402.5's special rule for property attributable to a predeceased spouse or domestic partner, are both cross-referenced by name in this clause's body but are not independently fetched, quoted, or verified by this document; a reader concerned with either provision should consult it directly.

NEXT IN LINE: SIBLINGS' ISSUE, THEN GRANDPARENTS AND THEIR ISSUE
If a decedent who dies intestate (or partly intestate, as to the part of the estate not passing to a surviving spouse or registered domestic partner) leaves no surviving issue and no surviving parent, Probate Code § 6402(c) sends that property to the issue of the decedent's parents — that is, the decedent's siblings, or the descendants of a deceased sibling — with those of the same degree of kinship to the decedent taking equal shares and those of a more remote degree taking their shares by representation under § 240. Only if there is no surviving issue, parent, or issue of a parent does § 6402(d) reach the decedent's grandparents: the property passes to the decedent's surviving grandparent or grandparents equally, or, if no grandparent survives, to the issue of the grandparents, again dividing equally among those of the same degree of kinship and by representation among those of a more remote degree.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(c) If there is no surviving issue or parent, to the issue of the parents or either of them, the issue taking equally if they are all of the same degree of kinship to the decedent, but if of unequal degree those of more remote degree take in the manner provided in Section 240. (d) If there is no surviving issue, parent or issue of a parent, but the decedent is survived by one or more grandparents or issue of grandparents, to the grandparent or grandparents equally, or to the issue of those grandparents if there is no surviving grandparent, the issue taking equally if they are all of the same degree of kinship to the decedent, but if of unequal degree those of more remote degree take in the manner provided in Section 240."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6402(c)-(d) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6402(c)-(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6402.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. This clause quotes subdivisions (c) and (d) of § 6402, the same statutory section already quoted for its introductory sentence and subdivisions (a)-(b) in the intestateshares_no_spouse_or_remainder_to_descendants_parents clause elsewhere in this document; that introductory "passes as follows" language, which subdivisions (c) and (d) both continue from, is not repeated in this clause's quote so that no subdivision of § 6402 is quoted more than once across this document. Subdivisions (e) through (g), reached only after grandparents and their issue are also exhausted, are quoted in the clause that follows this one rather than here. This clause does not independently verify Probate Code § 240's "by representation" method, referenced here only as a cross-reference.

THE FINAL CATEGORIES: ISSUE OF A PREDECEASED SPOUSE, NEXT OF KIN GENERALLY, AND IN-LAWS
Probate Code § 6402(e) through (g) sets out the last categories in California's intestate order, reached only if every closer category — issue, parent, issue of a parent, grandparent, and issue of a grandparent — is empty. If the decedent is survived by issue of a predeceased spouse or registered domestic partner, § 6402(e) sends the property to that issue, dividing it the same way as the earlier categories: equally among issue of the same degree of kinship to the predeceased spouse, by representation among those of a more remote degree. If there is no surviving issue of a predeceased spouse either, § 6402(f) reaches the decedent's next of kin generally, in equal degree, with a tie-breaking rule for collateral relatives of equal degree who trace through different ancestors: those claiming through the nearest common ancestor are preferred over those claiming through a more remote one. Finally, if there is no surviving next of kin and no surviving issue of a predeceased spouse, § 6402(g) reaches the parents of a predeceased spouse or registered domestic partner, or the issue of those parents.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(e) If there is no surviving issue, parent or issue of a parent, grandparent or issue of a grandparent, but the decedent is survived by the issue of a predeceased spouse, to that issue, the issue taking equally if they are all of the same degree of kinship to the predeceased spouse, but if of unequal degree those of more remote degree take in the manner provided in Section 240. (f) If there is no surviving issue, parent or issue of a parent, grandparent or issue of a grandparent, or issue of a predeceased spouse, but the decedent is survived by next of kin, to the next of kin in equal degree, but where there are two or more collateral kindred in equal degree who claim through different ancestors, those who claim through the nearest ancestor are preferred to those claiming through an ancestor more remote. (g) If there is no surviving next of kin of the decedent and no surviving issue of a predeceased spouse of the decedent, but the decedent is survived by the parents of a predeceased spouse or the issue of those parents, to the parent or parents equally, or to the issue of those parents if both are deceased, the issue taking equally if they are all of the same degree of kinship to the predeceased spouse, but if of unequal degree those of more remote degree take in the manner provided in Section 240."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6402(e)-(g) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6402(e)-(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6402.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. This clause quotes subdivisions (e) through (g) of the same § 6402 already quoted, in two other clauses elsewhere in this document, for its introductory sentence and subdivisions (a) through (d); no subdivision of § 6402 is quoted more than once across this document's clauses. Beyond subdivision (g), if no relative in any of these categories survives, the decedent's property escheats to the State of California under separate statutes this document does not cover. This document deliberately does not attempt to verify or restate every statutory nuance of these final, more rarely applicable categories — including the full mechanics of degree-of-kinship counting — beyond what § 6402's own text states.
